model:claude|title:discovering and explo.content_excerpt: Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to find critical vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. In this post, we share details of five attack chains, which led to remote code execution and other critical impacts with little to no user interaction. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities. We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our coordinated vulnerability disclosure , which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory. After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Our proof of concept launches the Calculator app from a stock default-configuration Chrome browser on macOS within seconds of the page loading, without any further user interaction: We have reported our findings to Google: 62 CVEs have been assigned and patched as of Chrome 156 , with all of them rated critical or high severity. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer. The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined. Apple acknowledged our report the same day we submitted it and implemented a fix promptly. That fix is available to users. model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . model:mistral|variant:large|title:welcom.content_excerpt: Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of 1M tokens . There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings). Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more! Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions. Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for. Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model. For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days. At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.”

Anthropic is running production inference and RL rollouts on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Historically, Trainium has been great for inference but not the best fit for research training. In inference, the model architecture changes at a much slower pace compared to training, where researchers iterate on many different experiments and ablations of model architecture and need a stack that covers a broad API surface. In the past, that is where Trainium fell short. The AWS Neuron team is aggressively working to change this pitfall with the biggest shift being moving towards a first-class, native PyTorch training experience. Gone are the days of sprinkling xm.step() through your training loop and wrestling with a bespoke XLA-style execution model. Trainium now runs PyTorch the way PyTorch users expect, in eager mode, with torch.compile and the standard APIs. The SemiAnalysis engineering team has been trying out the Trainium3 racks for the past couple of weeks and has found the experience to be great – we love the overall direction of where it is heading. To be clear, it isn’t perfect yet, and we have personally run into a couple of bugs ourselves. It’s nowhere close to the maturity of the CUDA ecosystem, but the direction is right. Their team is making rapid progress with the help of agentic coding. Furthermore, unlike other accelerator companies, where we had to fight tooth and nail to get their engineers a reasonably stable CI fleet, Trainium uses up to 80,000 physical cores allocated towards automated quality control. In this article, we walk through our experience on the Trainium3 TorchTitan and TorchNeuron stack, along with our experience of Trainium’s Neuron Explorer profiler, which is way better than both Nvidia’s and AMD’s profilers. story|title:artificial analysis v5 and t.content_excerpt: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregation metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. story|title:avartha fastest open weight.content_excerpt: Today, we are excited to announce Avartha. We are building the infrastructure to bring frontier-grade intelligence to real-time applications with open models that you control. Siri launched in 2011 with the promise of helping us “ get things done just by asking .” We want AI that can actually deliver on that promise, not just sound good. We now have models that can write software and reason through complex problems, but developers building voice agents have had to trade that capability for responsiveness. Even in mid-2026, GPT-4.1 remains the most popular model for building voice AI applications, simply because it is the only widely available model which has sub-1 second latency [5] . We believe that voice is poised to be the dominant interaction surface for all of computing in the future, and we want to build voice agents that operate at the frontier of AI capabilities and are a worthy complement to the intellect of their users. As the first step towards this goal, we are releasing Ava Zero 1 . story|title:can we trust llms to judge w.content_excerpt: Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. story|title:flare nvidia s dgx spark inf.content_excerpt: Flare is a local inference server for NVIDIA SM120/SM121 GPUs, built for long conversations, coding agents, and repeated tool use. Its goal is to make the memory, bandwidth, and compute in workstations and compact systems such as DGX Spark go further, while keeping generation responsive. Embrace the standard PyTorch ecosystem at build time; serve from Rust. Ignition uses PyTorch, Transformers, and FlashInfer/b12x to load models, tune kernels, compile forwards, and capture CUDA graphs into a runtime package. Helios, the Rust runtime, serves that package without Python. Compilation and graph capture finish before serving. Build on the model ecosystem. Reuse canonical model implementations wherever their dataflow fits, and specialize the parts that need different layouts or execution. Model development keeps the tools and libraries that make the Python ecosystem productive. Make memory and state explicit. Plan buffers and execution capacities ahead of time. Treat conversation state—including recurrent state alongside KV caches—as a whole, so reuse, branching, and resuming preserve it correctly. Keep the runtime small and shared. Model recipes own model computation; the runtime owns scheduling, cache storage, and request handling. A focused hardware and kernel stack keeps those boundaries manageable. vLLM covers a much broader range of models, hardware, and deployment patterns. Flare trades that breadth for a focused serving contract around selected models and local workloads. Flare is not, and will never, be a replacement for production inference englines like vLLM. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin . Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. story|title:how ai agents shape experts.content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. story|title:how to build evidence ground.content_excerpt: Agents working across an organization’s policies, manuals, wikis, tickets, and code must navigate knowledge scattered across systems and teams. Finding a relevant passage is only the start. They also need to determine which rules apply, what has changed, and how one source affects another. A persistent memory layer preserves knowledge and relationships for agents to reuse across tasks. Without it, agents often have to reconstruct that understanding on every question, making their work expensive and error-prone. This is especially challenging in banking and insurance, where policies and guidelines frequently amend or supersede one another. We tested OpenWiki , our open-source wiki compiler, as this memory layer. On questions requiring connections across sources, the wiki made the agent roughly 5x more accurate than search alone. Adding an evidence graph that connects wiki statements to supporting passages and links related sources improved accuracy a further 27% and doubled citation consistency. RAG pipelines often use semantic or hybrid search to retrieve isolated chunks, leaving agents to piece together how those chunks relate. We’ve explored improving retrieval with agentic RAG and graph-based metadata filtering , but finding relevant passages is only part of the work. Cross-source questions require tracing references, resolving conflicting rules, and understanding dependencies. Memory preserves that understanding so agents don’t have to rebuild it on every question. A compiled wiki provides that memory layer by synthesizing source material into linked pages that explain key concepts and their relationships. The wiki is updated as sources change, giving agents context they can reuse. OpenWiki , our open-source CLI built on Deep Agents , creates these wikis with citations back to the sources. We originally built it so coding agents wouldn’t have to rediscover architecture and code behavior on every task. Every OpenWiki statement rests on a claim , an assertion linked to supporting source lines and their hash. story|title:how to build proactive alway.content_excerpt: Ever hear of the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon? It's when you learn a word for the first time, and suddenly start hearing it everywhere. I think the same principle applies in software engineering: You learn about a simple, but effective, design pattern, and then suddenly start seeing it everywhere. We're seeing this happen with proactive agents, where we've noticed that nearly all of your favorite emerging proactive agentic systems are powered by a very simple mechanism: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case. The future belongs to proactive, always-on, ambient agents. Launches like Muse, Instinct, Dots, Claude Duet, Hone, and more reflect this. Crons power a few different capabilities that combine to make these agents proactive, personalized, and ambient — that is, they can perform tasks on their own, without being manually instructed. In this blog, we will go through the capabilities that crons unlock, the two core underlying parts you need in order to build agents like this, and then show examples of how you can do this in Managed Deep Agents . We’ve seen the impact crons can have. Proactivity is the new default for agent behaviour because of the breadth of new functions it unlocks. More than 70% of Managed Deepagent runs on LangSmith come from scheduled runs rather than a human typing a message. Implementing this partially involves running a background job to condense previous conversations into a denser form of memory. This is colloquially called “dreaming”. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. story|title:lakebase branching for ci cd.content_excerpt: Copy-on-write branching makes isolated copies of production data fast and cheap for CI/CD testing and agentic use cases. Snorkel AI builds data development tools for AI teams, used by expert data annotators and frontier model providers. In this specific use case, Snorkel ships code through a CI pipeline built on Kubernetes. Every open pull request, plus ad-hoc commits, gets its own ephemeral Kubernetes namespace (a "PR namespace"). Developers deploy their branch there and run the full test suite before merging. These tests are most useful when they run against real data. Snorkel's production database is an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Giving each PR namespace its own copy of that database was the hard part. Restoring a copy took about 20 minutes per environment, which is too slow when developers open PRs all day and the merge queue needs a fresh environment for each run. The alternatives (shared staging databases, trimmed fixtures, or synthetic data) bring back the problems production-like testing is supposed to solve: tests interfering with each other, stale schemas, and bugs that only show up with real data shapes. Lakebase is Databricks' serverless Postgres database. Its storage and compute are separate, and it supports branching: you can create a new, isolated, writable branch of a database from any point in time, the same way you create a Git branch. Branches are copy-on-write. Creating a branch is a metadata operation, so no data is copied when the branch is created. A new branch shares storage pages with its parent, and only the pages that the branch changes are written as new storage. For CI, this means: 1. Keep a fresh copy of production on the main branch. Lakebase is standard Postgres, so it works as a target for AWS DMS with no custom tooling. Snorkel points a DMS task at its production Aurora database and replicates it into the Lakebase project's main branch: a full load first, then ongoing change data capture that keeps main within about 2 minutes of production. Full LOB mode carries over the 10 to 20 MB JSONB values. The team already runs DMS, so there was no new replication pipeline to build or maintain. The main branch is the "golden copy" every PR branch starts from. 2. Create a branch when a PR opens. story|variant:small|title:rufous agent a.content_excerpt: rufous is an agent harness for 2B–12B models running on your own machine, either inside your editor or in its own web UI. While the model works, rufous keeps a Record of every Tool Call, one the model has no way of editing. Before a Turn ends, we hold the model’s report up against that Record. That is how we catch the file you named that never got written, the write you declined, and the refusal the model only half remembers. There is a single binary for macOS and Linux, and a zip for Windows. rufous is licensed under Apache-2.0, and you won’t need an account. Nothing about your usage is sent back to us. The short of it, is that rufous is built around the limits of a small model. We have measured it on models between 2B and 12B parameters, and every run starts with a Prefill of about 1,250 tokens , i.e. the system prompt plus nine core tool schemas. Every Tool Call the model makes passes through the five Rings of the Safety Gate before it touches your system. When a Turn ends with something missing, rufous places one Hold on the reply at most, and an honest “I couldn’t” always passes. Give a 4B model one clear instruction and it will usually carry it out. Three Turns into a conversation however, it turns out that it often does something close to what you asked, and then reports success. This is because a small model follows the most recent text in front of it, not the state of your files. rufous can’t make the model remember. What it can do is check. Every Tool Call is written to rufous’ own Record: which tool ran, the path or command it was given, whether it landed, and its exit code. Writes that you declined go on the Record too. From your instruction we work out which files you named with a write in mind, and where they should live. This is done with plain rules rather than a second model. The rules are tested against a labelled set, so that every change to them is measured. Did the model name a file it never wrote? Did it write the file in the wrong folder, or write the one you declined under another name? If so, the reply is held, along with a list of the paths that are missing. A Hold tells the model what is missing, and fires at most once per Turn. An honest “I couldn’t, because…” always passes. rufous will never loop a Turn in order to force an answer out of the model. story|ver:124|variant:moe|title:optimizi.content_excerpt: Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary. Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs: This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook . The evaluation used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has 42 layers: 35 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention (MLA) layers. Each MoE layer routes each token to eight of 512 routed experts, alongside one shared expert. For agentic workflows, Ling-3.0-flash provides a native 256K-token context window, expandable to 1M tokens. Compared with the previous Ling flash model, it improves long-horizon task stability, tool-calling accuracy, and harness compatibility. Developers can enable reasoning for complex agent tasks or disable it for latency-sensitive interactions. Improved spatial understanding supports constructing physical-scene grids and reasoning about relative positions in coding tasks. The baseline followed the official cookbook’s W4A8 configuration: FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, NVIDIA CUTLASS dense GEMM, and the –enable-fp32-lm-head option.
